blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A hook that must replace what the model sees as a tool's output has to work for built-in tools and for MCP tools, in both SDKs. Which field should it set?

options.text: additionalContext, since it overwrites the whole result with the text that is given
options.says: Ruled out because that field is for adding: "to append information to the tool result"

options.text: The newer successor setting, since the older one is limited to one server type and is deprecated
options.says: The page names the field (module 49, page 2): "To replace the tool's output before Claude sees it, set `updatedToolOutput`, which works for any tool in both SDKs."

options.text: updatedInput, since it rewrites the call before the model reads the answer
options.says: Ruled out because that field changes the call, not the result: "A replacement input for the tool"

options.text: permissionDecisionReason, since the model reads that text in place of the actual result
options.says: Ruled out because that text appears only on a refusal: "for a denial it is what the model reads"

questions.stem: Scenario S2. An adaptive loop halts when its planner issues a step it has already run. After a while the planner re-issues the step with different capitalisation. How should the check treat it?

options.text: Compare the exact bytes, since any difference between two steps shows real progress
options.says: Ruled out because the status names the cause: "The plan has stopped making progress"

options.text: Ignore case and surrounding spaces, since a faltering one seldom copies itself byte for byte
options.says: The page states it (module 50, page 2): "the repeated-step check ignores case and outer spaces, because a planner that has been stuck rarely repeats itself byte for byte".

options.text: Compare only the first word of each step, since the rest is only detail
options.says: Ruled out because the planner is the only judge of success: "The only success; the summary is the planner's"

options.text: Skip the check altogether and rely on the step limit alone to end the run
options.says: Ruled out because the limit is a backstop and not a check: "A loop that runs into it needs a progress check"

questions.stem: Scenario S2. An Edit call is refused because the target text appears three times in the file, and only one of the places should change. What is the first remedy?

options.text: Set replace_all, which changes just the line that was meant and no other
options.says: Ruled out because replace-all is for renames: "`replace_all` changes every occurrence, which is right for a rename and wrong when only one of three similar lines should change."

options.text: Read the file again and then retry the identical call
options.says: Ruled out because a second read does not change the match count: "The order of remedies is the order of risk."

options.text: Use Read and Write to rewrite the whole file
options.says: Ruled out because rewriting is the last resort: "which is the guide's fallback, changes the file by rewriting all of it"

options.text: Lengthen the anchor string until just the intended spot matches
options.says: The page orders the remedies (module 56, page 1): "A longer anchor changes only the occurrence you meant."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A developer has a deploy skill in ~/.claude/skills and the repository has its own deploy skill. Both places hold a skill called deploy, and the developer types the slash command without any prefix. Which one runs on /deploy?

options.text: The repository's, since committed files always override personal ones on every machine that uses the project
options.says: Ruled out because personal outranks project: "so a personal skill with the team's name silently replaces the team's version on your machine"

options.text: Neither, since a name clash disables both of them until one is renamed
options.says: Ruled out because a clash has a winner, and with both folders in place "`/deploy` runs the personal one" rather than disabling both.

options.text: Both, one after the other, starting with the committed one
options.says: Ruled out because a shared name keeps one version and a different name is what keeps both available: "The safe habit for a personal variant is a different name (`review-pr-mine`), which also keeps the team's version available to you."

options.text: The home-folder one, because that location outranks the committed one for a shared name
options.says: The page gives the order (module 58, page 1): "Enterprise over personal, and personal over project."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team rule seems ignored in a session. Which command shows what instruction files actually loaded?

options.text: /context, which lists every entry that is visible to the model
options.says: The page names the command (module 57, page 1): "`/context` lists the memory files that loaded into the session".

options.text: /memory, which lists the files that loaded and the ones that were skipped, with the reason for each
options.says: Ruled out because that command lists locations and opens them: "`/memory` lists the memory file locations and opens them in your editor, including ones you have not created yet."

options.text: /clear, which reloads every file from disk
options.says: Ruled out because clearing starts again and does not report: "Run `/clear` and start again"

options.text: /compact, which prints the instructions that survive summarising
options.says: Ruled out because compaction replaces text: "Compaction replaces older messages with a summary"

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A developer approves a plan in plan mode and picks the option that auto-accepts edits. Which two statements describe what approval does to the session? (Select two.)

options.text: It applies the plan to a copy of the repository before touching the real files
options.says: Ruled out because "Reading is free, and shell commands are controlled by the session".

options.text: It adopts the permission setting that the selected choice names
options.says: Approving "exits plan mode and switches the session to the permission mode each approve option describes" (module 59, page 1).

options.text: It ends the read-only phase
options.says: Approving "exits plan mode and switches the session to the permission mode each approve option describes" (module 59, page 1).

options.text: It restarts the session with the plan as its first message
options.says: Ruled out because "approve and start editing (in auto mode, or auto-accepting edits, or approving each edit by hand)".

options.text: It stays in plan mode and queues the edits until the end of the session
options.says: Ruled out because "In plan mode Claude researches and proposes, and does not change your source."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A developer asks Claude to write the code and then its tests from that code. The session produced twelve tests that all pass at once. Why is that weak?

options.text: Tests written after the code run more slowly than tests written before it was started by the team
options.says: Ruled out because the loop is the strength of tests: "Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes."

options.text: Claude cannot write tests for code that it wrote itself earlier in the same session
options.says: Ruled out because a check Claude can run is the aim: "Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare."

options.text: Generated tests are rejected by the runner unless a person has signed them off first
options.says: Ruled out because the developer writes or commissions them first: "The developer's part is to write, or have Claude write, the tests first and to give the target as the failing tests."

options.text: Cases born of one misreading confirm nothing, so the first checks should come from a person
options.says: The page states it (module 59, page 2): "A test written from the same misunderstanding as the code verifies nothing, which is why the first test cases come from a person or from the examples, and not from the code under test."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A skill's description and when_to_use text together run to several thousand symbols. What happens in the skill listing?

options.text: The skill is dropped from the listing until the wording is shortened by its author
options.says: Ruled out because the text is used to decide: "Claude uses this to decide when to apply the skill"

options.text: They are cut at 1,536, so the key use case belongs first
options.says: The page states it (module 58, page 1): "It should say what the skill does and when to use it, with the key use case first".

options.text: Only the description is shown and when_to_use is discarded from the listing
options.says: Ruled out because the two texts are treated as one: "the combined `description` and `when_to_use` text"

options.text: A model call summarises the wording before the skill is listed for use
options.says: Ruled out because the cut is a fact, not a removal of the skill: "is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing"

origin.section: The description is how a skill is found

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team has a repeatable procedure that should only enter context when someone starts it. Where does it belong?

options.text: In a project skill, whose body loads only when it is invoked
options.says: The page gives the table (module 58, page 2): "Its body loads only when invoked".

options.text: In the root memory file, which loads at launch
options.says: Ruled out because the root file is for every task: "Needed in every task of the project"

options.text: In a scoped rule with a paths list, which loads on a match between the files of the project
options.says: Ruled out because a scoped rule is for a kind of file: "About one kind of file, wherever it sits"

options.text: In the settings file as a hook that runs at session start
options.says: Ruled out because a hook is for fixed points: "it runs at a fixed point, whether or not the model remembers"

origin.section: Where each piece of guidance goes

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A developer wants short answers in every project on their machine, and the team does not. Where does that preference go?

options.text: In the project's root memory file, committed for the whole team to receive
options.says: Ruled out because a committed file is for the team: "Two kinds of line do not belong in a committed file."

options.text: In a local note beside the root file, ignored by version control on every machine
options.says: Ruled out because a local note is for one project: "A note about one project that nobody else needs, such as a sandbox address, goes in `CLAUDE.local.md`"

options.text: In the user-level memory document or the user rules folder in the home directory
options.says: The page states it (module 57, page 2): "A preference that follows you into every project, such as short answers, goes in the user file or in `~/.claude/rules/`".

options.text: In the managed policy file that the organisation distributes to its machines
options.says: Ruled out because a managed file reaches everyone: "Everyone on the machine, and individual settings cannot exclude it"

origin.section: Personal lines belong in personal files

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A developer asks Claude to refactor a module, and the session ends with code that looks finished but breaks a test. The prompt asked only to clean up the module and gave no further instruction. What was missing?

options.text: A longer prompt describing the module in much more detail than before
options.says: Ruled out because the model stops when the work looks done: "Claude stops when the work looks done"

options.text: A higher thinking budget so that the model reviews its own work harder
options.says: Ruled out because more room is not a new starting point: "a larger thinking budget, which gives the model more room to reason from the same starting point"

options.text: A second conversation that reviews the refactor once the session is over and reports back to the team
options.says: Ruled out because a second review in the same conversation shares the context: "a second review in the same conversation, which adds a third reader who shares the first two readers' context"

options.text: A runnable check, since otherwise an appearance of completion is the only signal
options.says: The page states it (module 71, page 2): "Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A review prompt holds standards, a few samples and the material under review. Which two statements describe the order? (Select two.)

options.text: Everything is interleaved, with each sample beside the part it resembles
options.says: Ruled out because "`<examples>` with one `<example>` per case, then `<diff>`".

options.text: The material goes first, so the model reads the input before any instruction
options.says: Ruled out because "The practice asks for the order criteria, examples, diff last, and its tests check it".

options.text: Samples come first, then the material, with the standards in a footer
options.says: Ruled out because that order "keeps the criteria and the examples together".

options.text: Rules lead, followed by worked cases each in its own tag
options.says: "Examples sit between the criteria and the input, each in its own tag, with the diff last" (module 61, page 2).

options.text: The input to judge sits last
options.says: "Examples sit between the criteria and the input, each in its own tag, with the diff last" (module 61, page 2).

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A batch finishes with some entries succeeded, some expired, and one rejected as an invalid request. What is the sound reaction?

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch to keep the results consistent with one another
options.says: Ruled out because a full resubmission pays twice: "Resubmitting the whole batch pays twice for work that is done."

options.text: Resubmit all the failures unchanged, including the one that was rejected as an invalid request
options.says: Ruled out because an invalid entry fails again: "sending it again fails again"

options.text: Keep the completed ones, resend the timed-out ones as they were, repair the faulty one
options.says: The page lists the reactions (module 63, page 1): "An entry that expired, was canceled, or hit a server error is resubmitted unchanged in the next batch".

options.text: Discard the batch and run all of the work synchronously instead
options.says: Ruled out because the discount is worth keeping: "The half price is a reason to move work that can wait."

origin.section: Failures: resubmit the failed items, and change what failed

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A bulk job submits batch entries that set stream to true. What happens?

options.text: Results stream back entry by entry as they finish, within the window of the batch
options.says: Ruled out because results are read from a finished batch: "A finished batch has a result per entry: succeeded, errored, canceled or expired."

options.text: The flag is ignored and results arrive after the window has closed
options.says: Ruled out because a batch finishes within a window: "A batch finishes within 24 hours (usually much sooner)"

options.text: It is refused with a validation error and the results come back as one file
options.says: The page lists it (module 63, page 1): "Three parameters are refused with a validation error: `stream: true` (the results come back as one file, not a stream)".

options.text: The batch is accepted but billed at the full price of the live API
options.says: Ruled out because the discount applies to work that can wait: "The half price is a reason to move work that can wait."

origin.section: What a batch request may and may not contain

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team proposes to log every tool result into the notes file during an exploration. Why is that wrong?

options.text: A file cannot be read back into a session once it has been written
options.says: Ruled out because later questions begin by reading it: "Later questions begin by reading the scratchpad"

options.text: Notes files are loaded into every session like an instructions file is
options.says: Ruled out because the instructions file is another thing: "It is not a replacement for the project's instructions file, which holds what is true of the project for every session"

options.text: Working memory should hold findings, not a transcript, which is what filled the window
options.says: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "it is not a transcript, which is the thing that filled the window in the first place".

options.text: Tool results contain nothing that is worth keeping for later questions
options.says: Ruled out because reading is what fills the window: "Exploration is the most context-hungry thing an agent does."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. On Wednesday an engineer wants to carry on Monday's exploration of the payments module as a single line of work, although two other sessions have run in that directory since. Which control fits?

options.text: Resume that session by its id, which adds to the original and keeps one thread
options.says: The page separates the two (module 51, page 1): "Resume to continue one thread; fork to branch it."

options.text: Fork the session, which keeps the whole history and carries on the work
options.says: Ruled out because a fork starts a second line: "a fork creates a new session with its own id, so the line of work now exists twice"

options.text: Continue the most recent session, which takes the newest one whatever it is
options.says: Ruled out because continue takes the newest: "Picks up the most recent session in the current directory and adds to it"

options.text: Start fresh with a prompt that asks the model to recall Monday from memory
options.says: Ruled out because the history is what holds the earlier analysis: "A session is the conversation history the SDK accumulates while your agent works."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. Two forks of one session each try a refactor in the same working directory. Which two statements follow the page? (Select two.)

options.text: A comparison that must not collide gives each branch its own copy of the code
options.says: "Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem", and "For a comparison that must not collide, fork for the analysis and let each branch work in its own copy of the code" (module 51, page 1).

options.text: Each fork gets a private copy of the whole directory, so the attempts are isolated
options.says: Ruled out because "If a forked agent edits files, those changes are real and visible to any session working in the same directory."

options.text: Branching copies the conversation and not the disk
options.says: "Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem", and "For a comparison that must not collide, fork for the analysis and let each branch work in its own copy of the code" (module 51, page 1).

options.text: Their edits are merged automatically when the sessions end
options.says: Ruled out because "Forking the session without isolating the files leaves both attempts editing the same checkout".

options.text: The second fork is rejected at once and a directory admits one branch
options.says: Ruled out because "Two forks that each try a refactor in the same working tree write over each other."

origin.section: What each way of going back costs

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A service runs an exploration on one machine, and an engineer wants to continue it on a CI worker. What limits this?

options.text: Sessions can be resumed only by the account that created them, whatever host is used
options.says: Ruled out because the limit is the machine and not the account: "You can resume from another directory on the same machine"

options.text: A saved session expires after one hour of idleness and cannot be reopened
options.says: Ruled out because idleness only changes the cost: a session "has been inactive for more than about an hour and is over 100,000 tokens"

options.text: Only the Agent SDK can resume sessions, never the command line
options.says: Ruled out because the command line can resume SDK sessions: "You can still resume one by passing its session ID to `claude --resume <session-id>`."

options.text: Saved conversations stay on the host that wrote them, so copy them or use a digest
options.says: The page states it (module 51, page 1): "Session files are local to the machine that created them."

origin.section: Where sessions live and how far they travel

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A process died while a tool call was running, and the session is resumed. What does the model see?

options.text: The operation flagged as interrupted before its outcome was stored, to verify
options.says: The page states it (module 51, page 2): the model "is told to check whether it took effect before running it again".

options.text: The call is finished again silently when the session resumes, without any notice
options.says: Ruled out because nothing runs again: "doesn't finish or run again when you resume"

options.text: The call is shown as succeeded, with no mark that it was cut short
options.says: Ruled out because a session does not mark old results: "Nothing in the session marks the old tool results as old."

options.text: The history is cut at the last completed message and the session carries on as normal
options.says: Ruled out because a session holds the conversation and not the world: "Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem."

origin.section: What a resumed session restores, and what it does not

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A team denies Write(secrets/**) to keep the agent from changing a folder. Why does that protect nothing?

options.text: Deny rules apply only to shell commands and are not applied to any of the file tools
options.says: Ruled out because the edit rules do cover file tools, so a deny is not limited to shell commands: "`Edit(path)` rules govern all built-in tools that write files, including `Write` and `NotebookEdit`"

options.text: Folders that hold credentials are exempt from deny rules for reading and for writing
options.says: Ruled out because no folder is exempt, and a read deny is the rule that protects such a folder fully: "A `Read(...)` deny rule also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path, including creating a new file there"

options.text: Deny rules are advisory, and the model may decide to ignore them when it sees fit
options.says: Ruled out because a matching deny is enforced, so the failure is the spelling and not an option the model has: "If a deny rule matches, the tool is blocked, even in `bypassPermissions` mode."

options.text: Path checks for modifications use the edit spelling, so a rule spelled the other way is never used
options.says: The page states it (module 56, page 2): "a `Write(path)` rule is never matched by the file permission checks".

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A team screens an agent's output for dangerous calls and runs it unattended whenever the screen is clean. Which two statements apply to relying on this alone? (Select two.)

options.text: Detection covers only what its authors anticipated, so a disguise slips past
options.says: "A scan finds what its authors thought of: a call spelled differently, built from strings or imported by name slips past it", yet "it refuses the obvious, it compares what the code does with what the proposal declares" (module 77, page 1).

options.text: Running it on every proposal costs too much, so it must be sampled
options.says: Ruled out because "and it costs nothing".

options.text: A clean result proves nothing about what the output declares
options.says: Ruled out because the table makes the declaration the thing to check: "Compare what the code does with the permissions declared, and refuse the difference".

options.text: Machine-written output cannot be read by any automatic check
options.says: Ruled out because "The gate in this module does read the code".

options.text: It still earns its place by refusing the obvious and checking what was declared
options.says: "A scan finds what its authors thought of: a call spelled differently, built from strings or imported by name slips past it", yet "it refuses the obvious, it compares what the code does with what the proposal declares" (module 77, page 1).

origin.section: A text scan is not a sandbox

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A tool design whose name breaks the required form also declares an effect that needs a person's sign-off. What should happen first?

options.text: It goes straight to the person, who can fix the name while approving
options.says: Ruled out because a flawed proposal does not reach a person first: "Otherwise a proposal with findings is sent back for revision."

options.text: It returns for revision, so approval goes to something worth reading
options.says: The page states it (module 77, page 2): "A revision comes before a gate, because a person should be asked to approve a proposal that is worth reading".

options.text: It is refused outright, with no chance of revision at all
options.says: Ruled out because a format error only sends it back: "Four things only send it back: a name that is not in the fixed form"

options.text: It is approved outright and fixed at a later review of the tool
options.says: Ruled out because only a clean proposal passes outright: "Only a proposal with none of these is approved outright."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A documentation tool's description is long, with its key rule in the last paragraph. What does Claude Code do with the text?

options.text: It reads all of it but shows only the first sentence of it to the user in the list of tools
options.says: Ruled out because the cut is a fact: "Descriptions and server instructions are truncated at 2,048 characters by default."

options.text: It summarises the description with a model call when the text is very long indeed
options.says: Ruled out because the advice follows from it: "Keep them concise, and put critical details near the start."

options.text: It truncates at 2,048 characters, so critical details should sit near the beginning
options.says: The page states the limit (module 55, page 2): "Claude Code truncates each tool description and each server's instructions at 2,048 characters by default".

options.text: It rejects the server at launch with an error message naming the limit in force
options.says: Ruled out because the page names the effect: "The exam rejects the length: Claude Code truncates at 2,048 characters, so what you put last may be cut."

origin.section: A description is what steers the model

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A skill from an installed plugin has the same folder name as a project skill. How can both be used?

options.text: The extension's is prefixed with its package label, so two commands exist
options.says: The page lists the location (module 58, page 1): "with the name prefixed by the plugin's name".

options.text: Only the project's skill stays and the plugin's one is dropped at install
options.says: Ruled out because the precedence list ranks only enterprise, personal and project skills, so it never drops a plugin skill at install: "Enterprise over personal, and personal over project."

options.text: Only the plugin's skill stays and the project's one is ignored while it is installed
options.says: Ruled out because the project skill stays available to its own audience, so installing a plugin does not ignore it: "Whoever works in the repository, through version control"

options.text: Neither runs until one of them is renamed to remove the clash
options.says: Ruled out because a shared name does not stop skills from loading: "A project-root skill and a nested one with one name both load".

origin.section: Where the file lives decides who gets it

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A user-level file and a repository-level file give conflicting style advice. Which two statements follow the page? (Select two.)

options.text: The user-level file loads last and personal preferences apply at the end
options.says: Ruled out because the files closer to the working directory come last: "instructions closer to where you launched Claude are read last".

options.text: Loading runs from the broadest scope to the most specific
options.says: The documentation lists the files "in load order, from broadest scope to most specific, so a project instruction appears in context after a user instruction" (module 57, page 1).

options.text: Memory is guidance with good delivery, not an override
options.says: The documentation lists the files "in load order, from broadest scope to most specific, so a project instruction appears in context after a user instruction" (module 57, page 1).

options.text: Neither file loads and the conflicting advice is dropped
options.says: Ruled out because "All discovered files are concatenated into context".

options.text: The more recently edited file loads last and the loader sorts by time
options.says: Ruled out because the order follows the folders: "ordered from the filesystem root down to the working directory".

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A skill lists disallowed-tools: Bash(rm *). What does that do while the skill is active?

options.text: It denies matching commands and keeps the shell available, since only a bare name removes it
options.says: The page states it (module 58, page 2): "A bare tool name like `Bash` removes the tool from Claude's context entirely".

options.text: It removes the shell from the available pool for the whole turn of the skill
options.says: Ruled out because only a bare name removes a tool: "only a bare name removes a tool"

options.text: It has no effect, since specifiers are ignored in the headers of skills
options.says: Ruled out because a scoped entry has an effect: "a scoped entry such as `Edit(src/**)` is a narrower rule that leaves the tool in place"

options.text: It blocks every command until the user sends the next message to the session
options.says: Ruled out because patterns are exact: "The patterns in `allowed-tools` are as exact as the rules in module 38"

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A developer wants the built-in exploring subagent to dig deeply into a tangled module. What can the caller request?

options.text: A level of thoroughness, from quick through medium to very thorough
options.says: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "The caller can ask for a thoroughness (quick, medium or very thorough)."

options.text: A write permission, from none to full access to the whole tree of the project
options.says: Ruled out because it is read-only: "with Write and Edit denied"

options.text: A larger window, from standard to extended for the long search
options.says: Ruled out because the cost of reading is the window: "Exploration is the most context-hungry thing an agent does."

options.text: A count of files to read, from ten up to a thousand files
options.says: Ruled out because the question has to be specific: "The question must be specific"

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A large exploration moves from mapping modules to tracing flows. How should the findings of the first phase reach the second?

options.text: A digest from the notes goes into the opening prompts of the later workers
options.says: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "The coordinator summarises the first phase's findings (from the scratchpad) and puts that summary into the initial prompts of the second phase's subagents."

options.text: Pass the full transcript of the first phase to each second-phase worker to lose nothing
options.says: Ruled out because the transcript is what filled the window: "It does not get the old transcript, which is what filled the first window."

options.text: Let the second phase rediscover them with fresh eyes
options.says: Ruled out because one phase starts from the next: "The findings of one phase are the starting point of the next."

options.text: Keep the first phase's workers running and reuse their windows
options.says: Ruled out because a worker does not inherit anything: "the brief must carry what the subagent needs, because it does not inherit the conversation"

origin.section: Summarise a phase, then inject it

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A manager tells a helper to explore the whole repository and gets back a long account. Which two statements describe what delegation needs? (Select two.)

options.text: The question has to be specific
options.says: "The question must be specific", and "the brief must carry what the subagent needs, because it does not inherit the conversation" (module 67, page 1).

options.text: The brief carries what the worker requires, since it inherits no conversation
options.says: "The question must be specific", and "the brief must carry what the subagent needs, because it does not inherit the conversation" (module 67, page 1).

options.text: The helper's window is too small for such a long search
options.says: Ruled out because "Subagents run in separate context windows".

options.text: The helper needs write access so that it can keep notes
options.says: Ruled out because "with Write and Edit denied".

questions.stem: Scenario S1. A long input holds twenty order summaries and a question. Where should the question and the key facts go?

options.text: The question at the start, to have the model read it before the summaries
options.says: Ruled out because the question belongs at the end: "The question at the end can improve quality on complex inputs."

options.text: The ask at the end, with a short digest of the essentials at the start
options.says: The page states it (module 64, page 1): "Put the long material first and the question last."

options.text: Both in the middle, where the attention of the model is strongest
options.says: Ruled out because "a long input's middle is where findings go missing".

options.text: The question repeated after every one of the twenty summaries
options.says: Ruled out because quoting before answering is another tool: "Asking the model to quote the relevant passages before answering is a fourth tool for long documents."
